items.title: L9: Judging whether a role really needs clearance
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK); Government Security Classifications Policy
items.body:
Deciding whether a role needs clearance, and at what level, is a judgement made by the sponsoring department, usually with its security advisers. It is not a formality, because clearance costs time and money, intrudes on the person and narrows the pool of people who can do the job. It is also not optional where the risk is real, because the harm from an unchecked person in a sensitive post can be severe.

A sound judgement asks a short series of questions. What can the post-holder see, reach or change? How often, and is it supervised? What is the worst plausible harm if the person were careless, coerced or hostile? Are there other controls, such as escort, system limits or need to know, that already reduce the risk? And would a lower level, or no check, manage it adequately?

Common errors run in both directions. Over-specifying happens when a department asks for SC because a previous holder had it, because the team likes the status, or because it is easier to ask for more. Under-specifying happens when a post is treated as low risk because the individual documents are OFFICIAL, ignoring aggregation or privileged system access, or when a temporary arrangement quietly becomes permanent.

Good practice is to record the reasoning, to revisit it when duties change, and to let a candidate ask why a level is required. Where the need is uncertain, the safer course is usually to seek the advice of the security team than to guess.

The decision should not be driven by who is in the post. It should be based on the access the post gives, whoever holds it.

When a post's duties grow, the level should be reviewed before the extra access is given, not afterwards.

questions.prompt: A team has always asked for SC for a post, but no one can say what the post-holder actually reaches. Which first step is most sensible?

options.text: Ask for DV instead, since the uncertainty suggests that the risk is higher than SC covers
Drop the requirement, since a post whose access nobody can describe must carry no real risk
Establish what the post can see, reach or change, how often and under what supervision, and then decide the level
Keep SC, because the previous holder had it and a change would be seen as lowering standards

questions.hint: The level should follow the access, so the access must be established first.

questions.prompt: Which reasoning is an example of over-specifying clearance?

options.text: Asking for advice from the security team because the access is unclear
Asking for CTC because the post gives unsupervised access to a sensitive site
Asking for baseline checks only because the post handles a few OFFICIAL documents
Asking for SC because the last holder had it and the team likes the status that comes with it

questions.hint: Copying a level without examining the access is over-specifying.

questions.prompt: Which situation is an example of asking for too little clearance for a post?

options.text: Treating a post as low risk because each document is OFFICIAL, though it holds privileged access to a large dataset
Choosing CTC for a post where access to SECRET material is only occasional and supervised
Recording the reasoning for a baseline-only post and reviewing it each year, so that creeping duties are noticed
Seeking the security team's advice before deciding on the level, because the access of the new post is not yet clear

questions.hint: Ignoring aggregation and system access under-specifies.

questions.prompt: A temporary arrangement lets an uncleared person see sensitive material 'just for a few weeks', and it continues for months. What is the main concern?

options.text: The arrangement is lawful for as long as the person is described as temporary
A temporary arrangement has quietly become permanent without the risk being reassessed
The department has done nothing wrong, because short arrangements need no control
The person should have been cleared to DV from the start in all such cases

questions.hint: Temporary exceptions need an end date and a review.

questions.prompt: Which question helps most in judging whether other controls can reduce the need for clearance?

options.text: Whether escort, system limits or need to know already keep the worst harm from occurring
Whether the person is popular with the team and has been a long time in post
Whether the department's budget for vetting this year is large enough to cover another clearance
Whether the vetting service is currently busy, so that a lower level would be processed more quickly

questions.hint: Existing controls change the residual risk.

questions.prompt: A candidate asks why the post needs SC. What is the best response from the department?

options.text: Say that all posts of that grade need SC and no explanation is required
Offer to lower the level if the candidate prefers a quicker process
Say that the level is confidential, so the candidate has no right to know the reason
Explain the access that the post gives and why a lower level would not manage the risk

questions.hint: Transparent reasoning builds trust and tests the judgement.

questions.prompt: When should the level be reviewed if a post's duties are growing?

options.text: At the next annual review, whatever the new duties are
When the post-holder asks for a review
Before the extra access is given, not afterwards
Only after a security incident has occurred

questions.hint: Review should precede the extra access.

questions.prompt: Which factor should not drive the choice of level?

options.text: The sensitivity of the material that the post is able to reach
The identity or standing of the person currently in the post
The degree of supervision that the post-holder works under
The potential harm that could follow if the access were misused

questions.hint: The level follows the post's access, not the holder.

questions.prompt: The sponsor is unsure whether a post needs CTC or SC. What is the most appropriate step?

options.text: Choose CTC, because it is quicker and the difference is small
Choose SC, because the higher level is always safer
Let the candidate pick whichever they prefer
Take advice from the security team before deciding

questions.hint: Uncertainty is a reason to seek expert advice.

questions.prompt: Why is it important to record the reasoning behind a level?

options.text: So that the decision can be revisited when duties change and can be explained if challenged
So that the reasoning can be shown to the press
So that the post can be graded higher
So that the record can replace the vetting process

questions.hint: A record supports review and accountability.

items.title: L9: Timing of declarations across the whole journey
items.source: HMG Baseline Personnel Security Standard; UK Security Vetting guidance; Civil Service Code
items.body:
Declarations are not one-off events. Different things need declaring at different times, and judgement is needed about which stage you are at.

At application and checks: anything the form asks for, answered as asked, including employment history, unspent convictions and, for clearance, the wider personal questions. Things that change between completing the form and starting should be reported when they arise.

Before and at the start: declarations of outside interests, relationships with suppliers or applicants, second jobs, and any conflict you can see coming. Many are asked at induction, and are repeated when anything changes.

During the job: significant changes of circumstance if you hold clearance, such as a new relationship, a serious financial problem, a new foreign link or a plan to live abroad. Conflicts that appear because your work changes, for example when your team begins to regulate a company in which you hold shares. Offers of gifts or hospitality, as they occur.

When leaving: planned outside appointments, where the business appointment rules apply, and handover of material and passes.

A useful test is 'what would a reasonable manager want to know now?' If something could affect your suitability, your access or your impartiality, say so when you notice it, not at the next review. Waiting for a convenient moment turns a declared matter into a late one, and late disclosure is judged more harshly.

Declaring early is not a confession. It lets the department manage the matter, which usually protects you as well as the organisation.

questions.prompt: You hold SC and begin a close relationship with someone who works for a company that bids for your department's contracts. When should you declare it?

options.text: After the relationship has lasted a year, when it is clear that it is serious and settled
At your next scheduled review, because that is the proper occasion for personal matters
As soon as the relationship looks likely to continue, without waiting for a review
Only when you are asked to take part in a particular bid by the company in question

questions.hint: Declare when it could affect impartiality, not at a convenient moment.

questions.prompt: In your first week you are told that your team will regulate a company in which you own shares. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Wait until a decision about the company is due before saying anything, since there is nothing to declare yet
Declare the shareholding at once so that the department can manage it
Sell the shares quietly and say nothing about having held them, so that the matter is closed
Say nothing, since owning shares is a private matter that the department has no reason to know

questions.hint: A conflict that appears because work changes should be declared promptly.

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the test 'what would a reasonable manager want to know now?'

options.text: Only matters that have already caused harm need to be mentioned, since others are speculation
Only matters that a form has already asked about need to be mentioned to the manager, since others are not required
Anything that could affect your suitability, access or impartiality should be said when you notice it
Only matters that are certain need to be mentioned, not possibilities that may never arise

questions.hint: The test looks ahead to relevance rather than formal requirement.

questions.prompt: Why is late disclosure judged more harshly than early disclosure?

options.text: It suggests the person chose a convenient moment and stopped the department managing the matter in good time
It always involves a larger sum of money than the same matter disclosed early
It is a criminal offence in every case, whereas early disclosure is not
It ends the person's right to take any further part in the process

questions.prompt: Between completing a clearance form and the decision, you take on a large new debt. What should you do?

options.text: Repay the debt as quickly as you can and then say nothing, since it will no longer exist
Tell the vetting team or your sponsor, since it is a significant change
Wait for the interview, if there is one, before raising it, so that it can be put in context
Say nothing until the decision, since the form was complete and accurate when you sent it

questions.hint: Changes during the process should be reported.

questions.prompt: An applicant realises after submitting the baseline form that an unspent conviction was left off. What is the right step?

options.text: Add it at the next review, if the post requires one, so that it is not forgotten
Wait to see whether the check finds it, since it may be recorded anyway
Declare it only if an interview raises it, because the form has already gone
Tell the checks team immediately and give the details

questions.prompt: Which of these changes would normally be reported by a clearance holder as it arises?

options.text: A change of mobile phone handset after a contract renewal
A plan to live abroad for a long period
A new hobby at weekends that involves other people
A change of supermarket for the weekly shop

questions.hint: Significant personal circumstances relevant to risk are reported.

questions.prompt: How should gifts or hospitality offers be handled in terms of timing?

options.text: Recorded only if their value is above a high threshold set by the department
Recorded only if they are accepted, since refused offers do no harm
Recorded as they occur, whether accepted or not
Collected and recorded together once a year at the annual review

questions.hint: Offers are recorded when they happen.

questions.prompt: What is the main benefit to the person of declaring early?

options.text: It lets the department manage the matter, which usually protects the person as well as the organisation
It increases the person's chance of promotion at the next board, since declarations are weighed as a sign of loyalty
It removes the need to declare anything else for the rest of the year, since the matter is then on record
It shows that the person is already an established member of the department

questions.prompt: You plan to leave for a private sector job related to your current work. Which step is appropriate?

options.text: Accept first and declare it on your last day, when it can do no harm
Declare it only if the new employer asks you to do so
Declare it only if the post is at a senior grade, since juniors are exempt
Check the business appointment rules and declare the plan before accepting

questions.hint: Planned appointments are declared in advance.

items.title: L9: Borderline matters: to declare or not
items.source: UK Security Vetting guidance; Civil Service Code; HMG Personnel Security Controls
items.body:
Many applicants and staff worry about the borderline cases: the things that are not obviously relevant but could be. The guiding principle is that you are not the best judge of relevance to your own case, and the cost of declaring something unnecessary is much lower than the cost of concealing something that matters.

Consider typical borderline matters. A discharged bankruptcy or a debt arrangement: declare, with dates and the current position. A past dispute with a former employer, such as a disciplinary action or a settlement agreement: declare the fact when asked about reasons for leaving, and take advice on any confidentiality terms, which do not override a duty to answer vetting questions honestly. A friend or relative with a conviction or a connection to a risky group: mention it if the form asks about associates, and explain the nature of the relationship. A foreign trip on an invitation from an organisation you do not know: report it, particularly if you hold clearance. A large unexplained gift or loan: declare it.

What vetting is not looking for is a spotless life. It is looking for honesty, reliability and resistance to pressure. A person who discloses a setback and shows how they dealt with it often looks more reliable than one with nothing to say.

Where you are unsure whether the form's wording covers something, ask the checks team or your sponsor, and keep a note of what you were told. If advice is not available, include the matter with a short explanation.

What you should not do is decide that something does not matter and drop it quietly. That decision belongs to the vetting officer.

questions.prompt: A discharged bankruptcy from some years ago is relevant to a vetting question on finances. What is the best approach?

options.text: Declare it with the dates and the current position
Mention it only if asked about it at an interview
Leave it out, since it is discharged and now in the past
Mention it only to a referee, who can speak for your character

questions.prompt: A settlement agreement with a former employer contains a confidentiality clause, and a vetting question asks why you left. What is the right approach?

options.text: Refuse to answer, because the clause forbids any mention of the matter to any third party
Answer honestly and take advice on the clause, since confidentiality terms do not override honest answers to vetting questions
Answer only if the former employer agrees to waive the clause in writing
Give a different reason, since the clause protects you from having to explain the real one

questions.hint: Honesty in vetting takes priority; take advice on the clause.

questions.prompt: A close friend has a conviction for fraud and the form asks about close associates. What should you do?

options.text: Leave the friend off the form, since the friend's conviction is not your own and says nothing about you
Include the friend only if they work in finance, since fraud would then be relevant
Include the friend only if you see them every week, since only regular contact counts
Include the friend where the form calls for it and explain the nature of the relationship

questions.hint: Relevance is for the vetting officer to weigh.

questions.prompt: You are invited on a trip abroad by an organisation you do not know, and you hold clearance. What is the sensible step?

options.text: Accept, but say nothing until you return, so that you can report what happened
Decline without mentioning why, since declining removes any risk
Report the invitation and take advice before accepting
Accept, since the trip is a private matter in your own time

questions.prompt: A relative gives you a large sum to help buy a house, and the vetting form asks about finances. What is the best approach?

options.text: Leave it out, since gifts from relatives are private family matters
Declare it only if the relative lives abroad, since only foreign sources matter
Leave it out until the money has been spent, when it can no longer be traced
Declare it, explaining the source and the purpose

questions.hint: Unexplained funds can raise questions, so explain them.

questions.prompt: What does vetting look for in a person with a past setback?

options.text: A letter from a previous employer apologising for the dispute
Honesty about it and evidence that they dealt with it reliably
A promise never to mention it again to anyone
A life without any setbacks of any kind

questions.prompt: Why is the applicant not the best judge of what is relevant to their own case?

options.text: They may underestimate how a matter looks from outside, and the vetting officer is trained to weigh it
Relevance is decided by the applicant's current manager, who knows the person's circumstances better than the vetting officer
The vetting officer must not accept anything that an applicant says
They tend to be dishonest when describing themselves, which is why vetting officers disregard what applicants say

questions.prompt: Which is the better course when the wording of a question is unclear?

options.text: Wait to see whether the question is asked again later in the process
Choose the interpretation that allows you to leave the most out
Ask the checks team or sponsor, and note the advice you were given
Guess, and correct it afterwards if you are challenged

questions.prompt: If no advice is available on a doubtful matter, what should you do?

options.text: Leave it out unless you are asked about it directly
Include it with a short explanation
Mention it to a friend first and follow their advice
Leave it out and say nothing, since it may be irrelevant

questions.prompt: What is the main problem with deciding quietly that something does not matter?

options.text: It means that the department will lose interest in the application
It means that the matter will be forgotten by the time the decision is made
That decision belongs to the vetting officer, and quiet omission looks like concealment
It means that the form will be shorter than other forms

items.title: L9: Accepting risk while clearance is pending
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK); Cabinet Office security policy
items.body:
When clearance is delayed, a department faces a choice between waiting and starting the person on restricted terms. This is a decision about accepting a limited, managed risk, and it should be made by someone with the authority to accept it, usually a senior manager advised by the security team, not by the new starter's line manager alone and not by the new starter.

The factors are the sensitivity of the work, how far access can be limited, the baseline checks already completed, whether there is any adverse information so far, the operational cost of waiting and the availability of supervision. If any adverse information has come to light, interim access is rarely appropriate until it has been resolved.

If restricted access is agreed, it should be explicit: what the person may see and may not, where they sit, who supervises them, which systems they can use, and for how long the arrangement lasts. These limits should be written down and understood by the person and their colleagues. Colleagues should know not to discuss restricted matters in the person's hearing, and not to treat the arrangement as a slight.

The arrangement ends when clearance is granted, refused or the agreed period expires. If clearance is refused, the person must lose the interim access at once, and the department must handle the situation fairly and confidentially, including looking at whether another role is suitable.

A department should resist informal drift: giving access 'just this once' because of a deadline, or letting an interim arrangement run on without review. Each exception makes the next one easier and makes the control less meaningful.

The person has responsibilities too: to keep to the limits, to tell the manager if they are asked to go beyond them, and to raise any concern.

questions.prompt: Who should decide whether to allow interim access while clearance is pending?

options.text: A colleague who holds the same clearance and understands the work, since they can judge the risk from experience
The new starter, who knows their own background better than anyone else involved and can judge the risk
The new starter's line manager alone, because they know the work best
A senior manager with authority to accept the risk, advised by the security team

questions.hint: Risk acceptance needs authority and advice.

questions.prompt: Which fact would make interim access least appropriate?

options.text: Adverse information that has come to light in the checks and has not been resolved
The work is mostly OFFICIAL, with little sensitive material
The baseline checks have been completed and cleared
The new starter will be supervised closely

questions.hint: Unresolved adverse information weighs heavily against interim access.

questions.prompt: What should be written down if restricted access is agreed?

options.text: Only the grade and salary of the post, which is the basis of the arrangement
What the person may and may not see, where they sit, who supervises them and how long the arrangement lasts
Only the name of the person's line manager and a contact number to use if there is a problem
Only the date on which clearance is expected, so that everyone can plan

questions.prompt: How should colleagues of a person on interim access behave?

options.text: Report the person to security every day, in case they have seen something
Ask the person to leave the room at every meeting, whatever the topic
Avoid discussing restricted matters in their hearing and not treat the arrangement as a slight
Tell the person everything so that they feel fully included in the team

questions.hint: Colleagues share responsibility for keeping to the limits.

questions.prompt: Clearance is refused. What must happen to the interim access?

options.text: It must end at once, and the department must handle the situation fairly and confidentially
It becomes permanent, since the person is already doing the work
It continues until the person finds another job, since the person cannot be left without work
It may continue until the end of the week to avoid embarrassment

questions.hint: Interim access depends on clearance still being pending.

questions.prompt: A deadline looms and a manager wants to let an uncleared person see a sensitive paper 'just this once'. What is the best response?

options.text: Allow it, if the person promises to forget what they read
Allow it, since the deadline is real and the paper is needed for one day only
Allow it, but ask the person to say nothing about it afterwards
Decline, and ask the person with authority whether a managed exception is possible, rather than breaking the limit informally

questions.prompt: Why is it unwise to let an interim arrangement run on without review?

options.text: The person will become too experienced in the work to be moved to another post when clearance is decided
Each unreviewed exception makes the next one easier and weakens the control
The person will build up an expectation of the higher pay that goes with cleared posts
The arrangement becomes a legal contract after three months

questions.prompt: A person on interim access is asked by a senior colleague to look at something beyond the agreed limits. What should they do?

options.text: Comply, but tell no one, so as not to embarrass the colleague
Refuse and leave the building at once
Decline politely, and tell their manager or the security team
Comply, since a senior colleague has the authority to decide

questions.hint: The person is responsible for keeping to the limits.

questions.prompt: Which statement about the operational cost of waiting is most accurate?

options.text: It is a legitimate factor to weigh, but it cannot by itself justify removing the limits
It is not a factor at all in the decision
It outweighs all other factors, since the service must continue
It applies only to the most senior posts

questions.prompt: When does interim access end?

options.text: When the line manager decides that it should end
When the person has been in post for six months
When the person has completed their induction programme
When clearance is granted, refused or the agreed period expires

questions.hint: Interim access ends with a decision or its time limit.

items.title: L9: Judging a conflict of interest: proportion and perception
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; Nolan principles (Committee on Standards in Public Life)
items.body:
Conflict of interest cases are judgement calls, and the guiding standard is the Civil Service Code together with the Seven Principles of Public Life, often called the Nolan principles: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty and leadership. A useful test is whether a reasonable, informed observer would think that your private interest could influence your public duty. It is the perception of the situation as well as its reality that matters, because public trust depends on both.

Proportion is the other half of judgement. A very small, remote interest in a large decision may need only a note; a close family business bidding for a contract you will score needs removal from the decision. The response should match three things: how close the interest is, how much influence you have, and how visible the decision is.

Typical responses, from light to heavy, are: record the interest, tell the people who need to know, limit your involvement in certain parts, hand the decision to someone else, or in a serious case change your role. A response that is too light leaves the risk; a response that is too heavy wastes skills and can penalise honest declarations.

Timing also matters. A conflict that is declared before a decision can be managed cleanly. One that emerges after a decision can force it to be reopened and damages trust.

Seniority adds responsibility. Leaders are expected to set an example, and a conflict involving a senior person is more likely to be scrutinised.

When unsure, ask. The question 'would I be comfortable if this were reported in the press?' is a rough but useful guide.

questions.prompt: Which test best captures the standard for judging a conflict?

options.text: Whether the decision has already been made and cannot be reversed
Whether you personally feel influenced by the interest when you take the decision
Whether any money has actually changed hands between you and the other party
Whether a reasonable, informed observer would think that a private interest could influence your public duty

questions.hint: Perception matters as well as reality.

questions.prompt: Which factors should the response to a conflict be matched to?

options.text: How close the interest is, how much influence you have, and how visible the decision is
The length of the contract and the date on which it begins, since longer contracts need stronger responses
Your grade, your age and the length of your service in the department
The size of your department and the budget it has for the year, which limit what you can ask for

questions.prompt: A very small, remote interest in a large decision is declared. Which response is likely to be proportionate?

options.text: Refer the person for prosecution under the Bribery Act
Remove the person from the department altogether
Record the interest and tell those who need to know
Ignore the interest, since it is too small to be worth recording

questions.hint: A light touch fits a remote interest.

questions.prompt: A close family business is bidding for a contract you will score. What is the likely response?

options.text: Scoring it last, after everyone else, to reduce the risk of influence
Removal from the decision, with the interest recorded
Scoring only the part of the bid that does not involve the family business
A note on the file and no change to your role in the scoring

questions.hint: Close interest and direct influence need removal.

questions.prompt: Why can a response that is too heavy be a problem?

options.text: It makes the underlying conflict worse
It always breaks the law on employment
It is forbidden by the Civil Service Code
It wastes skills and can discourage people from declaring honestly

questions.prompt: Why does timing matter in dealing with a conflict?

options.text: Declared before a decision it can be managed cleanly, but after the decision it may force it to be reopened
Timing has no effect on how a conflict is judged, since the interest is the same whenever it is declared
Early declarations are normally ignored, since nothing has yet happened that needs managing
Later declarations are treated as more honest because they are more carefully considered

questions.prompt: Which of the seven principles of public life is most directly engaged by a hidden conflict?

options.text: Selflessness alone
Accountability alone
Openness and honesty
Leadership alone

questions.hint: Hiding a conflict breaches openness and honesty.

questions.prompt: Why is a conflict involving a senior person more likely to be scrutinised?

options.text: Senior people cannot have conflicts, so any report is suspect
Leaders are expected to set an example, and their decisions are more visible
Senior people are exempt from the duty to declare conflicts
Senior people are more likely to be dishonest than junior ones

questions.prompt: Which is a rough but useful guide when you are unsure about a situation?

options.text: Whether the amount of money involved is small enough to be of no real interest to anyone
Whether your friends and family would approve of what you did when they heard about it
Whether the same matter would be lawful in another country
Whether you would be comfortable if the matter were reported in the press

questions.prompt: What is the best step if you are unsure whether something is a conflict?

options.text: Ask your manager or the relevant advisers before acting
Decide privately and act, then tell no one
Ignore it, since doubt means it is probably not a conflict
Wait for someone else to notice and raise it

items.title: L9: A colleague's lapse: report, support or ignore?
items.source: Civil Service Code; Government Security Classifications Policy; ICO guidance
items.body:
Seeing a colleague break a security rule is uncomfortable. You may like them, the lapse may seem small and reporting may feel like betrayal. The Civil Service Code, however, expects integrity and responsibility for the protection of information, and security depends on everyone playing their part.

A sensible judgement has two steps: what is the risk, and what is the right route?

On risk, ask how sensitive the information is, how likely it is to have been seen by someone who should not, whether it is a one-off or a pattern, and whether the colleague is aware. A password written on a note under a keyboard, left in a locked office, is a small lapse. A password shared with a contractor, or a sensitive file sent to a personal account, is a larger one. A pattern, or a lapse that has already led to exposure, is more serious.

On route, the first step with a minor, first-time lapse is often a quiet word: 'I noticed you left your screen unlocked; it is easy to do.' That corrects the behaviour without a formal process. If the lapse is more serious, has caused exposure, is repeated, or the colleague dismisses it, report it through the department's route, usually to a line manager or the security team. You do not need proof; you need to report what you saw. Reports made in good faith are protected, and you should not investigate yourself.

What you should not do is ignore it because it is awkward, or discuss it with other colleagues, which spreads the problem and may be unfair to the person.

Where an incident has already happened, such as a lost device, the person responsible should report it at once, and you should encourage them to do so, or report it yourself if they will not.

questions.prompt: You see a colleague's screen unlocked and visible to visitors in an open office, as a first-time lapse. What is a proportionate first step?

options.text: Taking a photograph of the screen as evidence of what was visible
A quiet word with the colleague, locking the screen if needed
Telling the whole team at the next meeting so that everyone learns
Reporting the colleague formally to the security team on the same day

questions.hint: A quiet word fits a minor first-time lapse.

questions.prompt: A colleague sends a sensitive file to a personal email address 'for convenience'. What is the best response?

options.text: Delete the email from the colleague's account to remove the evidence
Ask the colleague to send you a copy as well, so that you can check it
Report it through the department's route, since the information has left the system
Ignore it, since the colleague meant no harm and it was done for convenience

questions.hint: Exposure of sensitive information needs reporting.

questions.prompt: What most clearly distinguishes a serious lapse from a minor one?

options.text: The time of day at which it happened, since out-of-hours lapses are always more serious
Exposure of sensitive information, repetition, or the colleague dismissing the concern
The colleague's popularity with the team, since popular colleagues are less likely to repeat a lapse
The colleague's seniority in the department

questions.prompt: Do you need proof before reporting a lapse?

options.text: You must have the approval of the colleague concerned
You must have a witness who saw the same thing
You report what you saw, and reports made in good faith are protected
You must have photographs of what happened

questions.prompt: Why should you not discuss a colleague's lapse with other colleagues?

options.text: It breaks the Official Secrets Act automatically, whatever is said and to whom it is said
It is a criminal offence in every case, because the lapse itself is a matter of confidential information
It is permitted only for managers and senior staff
It spreads the problem and may be unfair to the person, while the right route is the manager or security team

questions.hint: Discussion is not a proper route.

questions.prompt: A colleague loses a work phone and says they will 'look for it first'. What should you encourage?

options.text: Reporting the loss at once through the security route
Buying an identical phone so that nobody notices
Checking the car and the office first, and reporting only if it is not there
Waiting a day in case it is found at home

questions.prompt: A colleague will not report a serious incident. What should you do?

options.text: Try to resolve it privately so that nobody is embarrassed
Wait for the colleague to change their mind in their own time
Say nothing, since it is their responsibility and not yours
Report it yourself through the department's route

questions.hint: You may need to report it yourself.

questions.prompt: Why is a pattern of lapses more concerning than a single one?

options.text: It is always intentional rather than careless
It suggests a lack of care or understanding that a quiet word has not fixed
It proves the colleague is working for another state
It shows the colleague is more senior than others

questions.prompt: How should you view a good-faith report about a colleague?

options.text: As an attack on the colleague's career which is likely to damage their prospects for good
As a betrayal of the colleague that damages the team
As part of everyone's responsibility to protect information, not as betrayal
As gossip that should be discouraged, since it is unfair to talk about a colleague behind their back

questions.hint: Reporting protects information and often the colleague too.

questions.prompt: Which action would be wrong when you spot a lapse?

options.text: Investigating it yourself by searching the colleague's desk
Having a quiet word about a minor first-time lapse
Reporting what you saw to the proper route
Noting the time and what you saw

items.title: L9: Your own lapse: what to say and when
items.source: Civil Service Code; ICO guidance on personal data breaches; HMG security incident guidance
items.body:
Everyone makes mistakes with information at some point. The test of professionalism is what you do next. A good response is fast, factual and honest, and it helps the organisation limit the harm.

Fast means reporting as soon as you realise, because early action can often recover a message, lock a device or warn a recipient, and because the organisation's own deadlines, such as the 72 hours for notifying the Information Commissioner's Office where a breach is likely to risk individuals, run from when it becomes aware. Factual means saying what happened, what information was involved, who might have seen it and what you have already done, without minimising or speculating. Honest means including the parts that are embarrassing: that you sent it to the wrong address because you did not check, that you used a personal account, that you noticed yesterday and did not report.

It is natural to feel shame, and to want to fix it quietly. That instinct is the one to resist. A quietly fixed mistake that later comes to light looks like concealment and is treated as a conduct matter, whereas a promptly reported mistake is usually treated as a learning event.

After reporting, cooperate with the response, do not delete anything without direction, and keep a short note of what you did. If you are anxious, ask for support. Departments provide welfare support and managers should treat reporting as responsible.

Reflect afterwards. What made the mistake likely: haste, an unclear process, a confusing system? Telling your manager what could be changed is part of learning.

If the incident is serious and repeated, it may lead to formal action, but honesty is always counted in your favour.

questions.prompt: You realise at 5pm that you sent a spreadsheet of customer data to the wrong external address at noon. What is the best course?

options.text: Report it at once, saying what happened and that you noticed late
Wait until tomorrow so that you can check the facts before you report
Delete your sent message and say nothing, since the damage is done
Try to recall the message first and report only if that fails

questions.hint: Prompt, honest reporting, including the delay.

questions.prompt: Which description best fits a good report of a lapse?

options.text: Long, detailed and defensive
Fast, factual and honest
Delayed, careful and polished
Short, vague and apologetic

questions.prompt: Why should you include the embarrassing parts of the story in a report?

options.text: The embarrassing parts are what the department is most interested in
Embarrassing parts are always required by law, which is why they appear in every formal report
Embarrassing parts reduce the penalty automatically, so that the more embarrassing the account the lighter the outcome
A partial account can mislead the response, and looks like concealment when the rest emerges

questions.prompt: Why does the organisation's own clock matter to your reporting?

options.text: The clock starts only when the person is disciplined
The clock starts only when the ICO is told
Its notification deadlines run from when it becomes aware, which depends on your report
The clock is irrelevant to individual staff

questions.prompt: What is the main risk of quietly fixing a mistake?

options.text: The customer may complain about the correction and so draw attention to the original mistake
If it later comes to light it looks like concealment and is treated as a conduct matter
The fix may be done incorrectly, which would make the damage to the customer worse than before
The manager may be annoyed that you did not ask

questions.prompt: After reporting, what should you do?

options.text: Delete anything that might be embarrassing, to limit the damage
Investigate the cause yourself and report the result
Cooperate with the response, keep a short note, and not delete anything without direction
Wait to be contacted and say nothing more until then

questions.prompt: You feel anxious after a mistake. What is appropriate?

options.text: Ask for support, since welfare support exists and reporting is responsible behaviour
Resign, to avoid the difficulty that is likely to follow from having made a serious mistake
Take leave without telling anyone why, so that the stress has time to pass before it is discussed
Keep it to yourself, since anxiety will pass

questions.prompt: What is a useful reflection after an incident?

options.text: Whether anyone noticed, so you know how worried to be
Whether the matter will be forgotten, so you can move on
Whose fault it was, so that the right person is told
What made the mistake likely, such as haste or an unclear process, and what could change

questions.prompt: How does honesty count when a serious incident leads to formal action?

options.text: It increases the penalty, since it admits fault
It is irrelevant to formal action
It is counted in your favour
It is ignored, since only the facts matter

questions.prompt: Which statement about a mistake reported promptly is most accurate?

options.text: It is always ignored by the department, since a report made late or early makes no difference
It is usually treated as a learning event rather than a conduct matter
It is always treated as a disciplinary matter, because any breach is a conduct issue however it comes to light
It is always reported to the police

items.title: L9: Changes in a colleague that cause concern
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK); Civil Service Code; NPSA guidance on insider risk
items.body:
Most security problems are caused by people who are under strain, careless or unaware, not by people who intend harm. The same signs can mean very different things, and the right approach combines care for the person with care for the organisation.

Typical changes that deserve attention include sudden unexplained financial difficulty or unexplained wealth, a marked change in behaviour or mood, a pattern of working unusual hours with no reason, interest in material outside the person's work, repeated breaches of simple rules, new or unexplained foreign contacts, or signs of drug or alcohol problems affecting work. No single sign proves anything. Illness, bereavement, family trouble and money worries are common and are not wrongdoing.

The sensible response depends on the combination. If you are worried about a colleague's wellbeing, the first step is a kind, private conversation, or a quiet word with their manager. If what you see suggests a possible security risk, such as access beyond need or an unexplained approach by an outsider, report it through the department's security route, giving facts and not conclusions. The security team can combine your report with other information and decide what to do. You are a witness, not a judge or investigator.

Guard against two errors. One is ignoring a concern because it feels disloyal or because you might be wrong. The other is jumping to conclusions about someone because of their background, nationality, personal life or appearance. Reports should rest on behaviour, not on identity, and unsupported suspicions harm both the person and the process.

Managers have a particular duty to notice and to support. Early help, such as welfare support or a conversation about money problems, often prevents a worse outcome.

Reports made in good faith are protected and handled in confidence.

questions.prompt: A colleague who was previously punctual starts coming in at odd hours and asks about projects outside their work. What is the best judgement?

options.text: The behaviour should be discussed with the colleague's friends
The combination proves the colleague is a spy and should be confronted
The behaviour is none of your business and should be ignored
Neither sign proves anything, but the combination is worth passing on factually to the security route

questions.hint: Combinations of signs justify a factual report.

questions.prompt: A colleague appears distressed and mentions money worries. What is the sensible first step?

options.text: A kind, private conversation, or a quiet word with their manager about support
Avoiding them for a while, so as not to become involved in something that is not your business
Reporting them as a security risk immediately
Telling the whole team about the money worries so that everyone can help out

questions.hint: Wellbeing concerns call for care first.

questions.prompt: What should a report to the security route contain?

options.text: A list of their personal habits
Your opinion of the person's character
Facts about what you saw, not conclusions about the person
A guess about their motives

questions.prompt: Which basis for suspicion should never be used?

options.text: The person's nationality, background, personal life or appearance
Access to records beyond what the person's work needs
A pattern of repeated rule breaches after reminders
An unexplained approach by an outsider

questions.prompt: Why is ignoring a concern a mistake?

options.text: Ignoring a concern makes it disappear
Ignoring is rude to the colleague
Ignoring a concern is a criminal offence
The person may need help or the organisation may be at risk, and fear of being wrong is not a reason to stay silent

questions.prompt: What is your role when you report a concern?

options.text: Judge, deciding whether the colleague is guilty and what should be done about them
Witness, not judge or investigator
Prosecutor, collecting evidence to build a case against the colleague
Investigator, gathering evidence about the colleague's behaviour before you report it

questions.hint: Leave investigation to the right team.

questions.prompt: Which of these is a common non-wrongdoing explanation for changed behaviour?

options.text: A wish to join a competitor
A plan to leak information
Illness, bereavement, family trouble or money worries
A dislike of the team

questions.prompt: What particular duty do managers have in this area?

options.text: To notice and to support, since early help often prevents a worse outcome
To discipline anyone who changes behaviour
To report every change in a colleague's behaviour to the press office, for the department's protection
To ignore private matters completely, since they are not the employer's concern in any circumstances

questions.prompt: How are good-faith reports handled?

options.text: They are published to the team
They are protected and handled in confidence
They are kept for ever on the person's file
They are passed to the person concerned

questions.prompt: Which approach avoids both errors, ignoring a concern and jumping to conclusions?

options.text: Telling other colleagues what you suspect
Telling the person directly what you suspect, so that they have a chance to explain themselves
Saying nothing and watching for a few weeks, so that there is more evidence before you act
Reporting observed behaviour factually and leaving assessment to the security team

items.title: L9: What the checks and clearance process protects
items.source: HMG Personnel Security Controls (GOV.UK); Civil Service Code; Cabinet Office guidance
items.body:
It is easy to experience pre-employment checks and vetting as paperwork or intrusion. A fuller view is that they protect several things at once.

They protect the public: people's personal data, benefits, safety and the services they depend on are only as safe as the people who handle them. They protect information and assets: government holds material whose loss could harm national security, the economy, individuals or international relationships. They protect the integrity of decisions: if staff can be bribed, pressured or compromised, public decisions can be distorted. They protect colleagues: one insider incident can put others at risk and harm trust in the whole service. And they protect the individual: checks that are fair and evidence-based, and an environment where people can declare problems and get support, reduce the chance that someone is exploited or blamed unfairly.

Good personnel security is therefore proportionate, fair and honest. Proportionate means asking only for what the risk justifies. Fair means treating similar cases alike, giving a chance to explain, and not discriminating on grounds such as race, religion, sexual orientation or disability. Honest means that the department too is truthful about what it asks and why.

A frequent mistake is to say 'I am trustworthy, so the checks are pointless'. The checks do not assume anyone is untrustworthy. They provide assurance that does not depend on any one person's word, including that of the person being checked. Another mistake is to treat clearance as a statement of character. It is a risk assessment for a particular role at a particular time.

Finally, personnel security is a continuing activity. A clearance reflects the position when it was granted, and its value depends on people continuing to be open about changes.

questions.prompt: A new starter says, 'I am honest, so these checks are pointless.' Which reply best explains why checks matter?

options.text: Checks give assurance that does not rest on any one person's word, including the person being checked
Checks are a test of honesty that most people fail, so everyone has to take them
Checks assume that everyone is dishonest, which is why they are repeated
Checks are mainly for the benefit of the vetting service, which needs the work

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes what clearance is?

options.text: A certificate of good character that stays with the person for life
A reward for long service in the department
A permanent right to see sensitive information at the level granted
A risk assessment for a particular role at a particular time

questions.hint: Clearance is a role-based risk judgement.

questions.prompt: Which of these is something the process protects?

options.text: The secrecy of every piece of government work
The public's personal data and the services that they rely on
The reputation of individual managers, whose decisions would otherwise be exposed to criticism
The pay and conditions of senior staff in the department, which depend on clean records

questions.hint: The public is one of the protected interests.

questions.prompt: How can the process protect the individual being checked?

options.text: By keeping their details secret from everyone, including the vetting officer
By ending all checks after the first year of service
Fair, evidence-based checks and an open culture reduce the chance that someone is exploited or blamed unfairly
By promising clearance to everyone who applies

questions.prompt: What does 'proportionate' mean in personnel security?

options.text: Asking only for what is quick and easy to check
Asking for the same checks for every post whatever the risk
Asking only for what the risk justifies
Asking for as much information as possible, in case it is needed

questions.prompt: Which of these is part of fairness in checks?

options.text: Treating senior people more leniently than junior people
Treating similar cases alike and giving a chance to explain
Withholding the reasons for a decision to protect the vetting officer
Rejecting anyone with a past setback, whatever the circumstances

questions.hint: Consistency and a chance to explain.

questions.prompt: Which of these must not be a basis for discrimination in the process?

options.text: Race, religion, sexual orientation or disability
The honesty of an applicant's answers, which is something the checks are designed to test
The applicant's willingness to explain a matter
The sensitivity of the access that the post gives, which is central to the level chosen

questions.prompt: Why does personnel security need to continue after clearance is granted?

options.text: Clearance is only a formality in any case
Clearance expires after a day and has to be renewed every morning
Clearance is only for new starters
A clearance reflects the position when it was granted, and its value depends on people reporting changes

questions.prompt: Why can one insider incident harm more than the person involved?

options.text: It increases pay for the people involved, because they are compensated for added scrutiny
It makes all colleagues more senior, since a serious incident leads to extra responsibility
It can put colleagues at risk and damage trust in the whole service
It affects only the person who caused it

questions.prompt: Which statement best summarises good personnel security?

options.text: Proportionate, fair and honest
As quick as possible
As strict as possible
As secret as possible

items.title: L9: Speaking and writing in a professional capacity: borderline cases
items.source: Official Secrets Act 1989; Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code
items.body:
Civil servants are encouraged to engage with their professions, give talks, publish research and take part in public life, provided that they respect their duties. The difficult cases lie at the edges, and a general method helps.

First, ask whether the content uses official information that is not already public. If so, authority is required, not just good intentions. Second, ask whether you would be speaking as a civil servant. If you are identified as one, or the subject is your department's work, you need approval under the department's rules, usually through your line manager and the press or communications office. Third, ask whether the topic touches policy, ministers or politics. Even if you add that the views are your own, the impartiality expected of civil servants and the Civil Service Management Code limit public comment on political matters and policy, particularly for senior and sensitive roles.

Examples. A talk at a conference about general professional methods is usually fine, but if it draws on internal data it needs clearance. An academic paper using department data needs approval and sometimes a data sharing agreement. An article after leaving needs checking against the Official Secrets Act and any continuing obligations. Giving evidence to a parliamentary committee as a civil servant is done on behalf of the department and with its agreement. Contacting an MP privately about your own department's work is not a route to disclose official information.

When you are unsure, ask early. Approval takes time, and a refusal at the start is better than a breach at the end.

If you think the public ought to know something, use the proper routes for raising a concern. Remember that the Official Secrets Act 1989 has no public interest defence.

questions.prompt: You are invited to speak at a conference about general methods in your profession, using no internal data. What is the likely position?

options.text: Always forbidden to civil servants, whatever the subject, unless a minister has given written approval
Fine, but only if you speak under a pen name, so that the department's name is not linked to you
Fine only for senior civil servants, who are trusted to judge
Usually fine, though approval under the department's rules may still be needed if you are identified as a civil servant

questions.hint: General professional talks are usually acceptable.

questions.prompt: You want to include internal department data in your conference talk. What is required?

options.text: Permission from the audience, who must be told what the data is
Authority, since the data is official information that is not already public
Nothing, as long as the data is not sensitive
A disclaimer on your slides saying the views are your own

questions.prompt: Why does 'views my own' not remove the need for approval?

options.text: It does remove the need, if the disclaimer is placed on the first slide
Impartiality and the Management Code limit public comment on policy and political matters, and a disclaimer does not override duties
It applies only to private conversations and not to written work, which has to go through approval
It is a legal protection that covers any statement made in public

questions.prompt: An academic wants to publish a paper using your department's data. What is the right approach?

options.text: Seek approval and, where needed, a data sharing agreement
Publish under another name to protect the department
Publish first and seek approval afterwards
Send the data informally so that the work can start

questions.hint: Formal approval and agreements are needed.

questions.prompt: A civil servant plans to write an article after leaving. What is the right step?

options.text: Publish freely, since they no longer work there and so owe the department nothing further
Ask a friend in the department to read it casually, which is enough to check that nothing is wrong
Publish only if the article is flattering to the department
Check it against the Official Secrets Act and any continuing obligations before publishing

questions.prompt: How does evidence to a parliamentary committee by a civil servant usually operate?

options.text: Only after the civil servant has left the department
On the civil servant's own initiative and in a personal capacity
On behalf of the department and with its agreement
Only through the press office, which answers on the civil servant's behalf

questions.hint: It is done for the department.

questions.prompt: You email your MP privately about your department's work, including unreleased details. What is the position?

options.text: It is fine if the MP belongs to the governing party
It is fine, since MPs may receive any information
It is not a proper route for disclosing official information
It is fine if you mark the email private

questions.hint: MPs are not a route for official information.

questions.prompt: Why is it better to ask early about a talk or article?

options.text: Asking is not required for talks, since only written articles need approval
Early requests are always refused, so it is better to wait until the event is certain
Approval is always quick and automatic
Approval takes time, and a refusal at the start is better than a breach at the end

questions.prompt: You believe the public should know something that is protected. What should you do?

options.text: Use the proper routes for raising a concern
Post it anonymously on a website
Tell a journalist informally, without naming yourself
Publish it, since the public interest justifies it

questions.hint: The 1989 Act has no public interest defence.

questions.prompt: What is the first question in the general method for borderline speaking and writing?

options.text: Whether the event is abroad
Whether the content uses official information that is not already public
Whether you are being paid
Whether the audience is large

items.title: L9: When a senior person asks you to bypass a control
items.source: Civil Service Code; Government Security Classifications Policy; Public Interest Disclosure Act 1998
items.body:
One of the hardest tests of judgement for a junior civil servant is a request from a senior colleague to bypass a security or integrity control. Examples include sending a sensitive document to a personal email 'because the system is slow', sharing a login, accessing records without a work reason, or skipping a conflict declaration. The person is senior, the reason sounds practical and refusing feels risky.

The Civil Service Code is clear that civil servants should act with integrity and must not misuse official information, and that seniority does not change that. It also provides support: you can raise the matter with your line manager, a nominated officer or, in the last resort, the Civil Service Commission, and you should not be penalised for raising a concern properly.

A workable approach is to separate the issue from the person. First, decline the specific action politely and briefly, without accusing: 'I am not able to do that, as it is outside the rules. Can we find an approved way?' Second, offer an alternative that meets the need, such as a secure transfer or a request to the system owner. Third, if the person insists, or the request is serious, record what was asked and report it through the proper route. Fourth, keep notes with dates.

It may help to ask yourself three questions: Is the action permitted by policy? Would I be comfortable explaining it to the security team? Would the harm if it went wrong be serious?

If you have already complied under pressure, report that too. Telling your manager you were asked to do something and did it is better than hoping it is never noticed.

Senior people also have a duty to listen. A polite refusal is often received better than expected.

questions.prompt: A senior colleague asks you to send a sensitive document to their personal email 'because the system is slow'. What is the best response?

options.text: Decline politely, explain that it is outside the rules, and offer an approved alternative
Send it, but copy it to your manager so that someone is aware what has been sent and why
Send it, then delete your sent copy so that no record remains on the department's system
Send it, since the colleague outranks you and has accepted the risk

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly describes the effect of seniority on the rules?

options.text: Seniority applies only to staff below you
Seniority matters only in emergencies
Seniority does not change the rules or your duty of integrity
Seniority overrides the rules for sensitive material

questions.prompt: Which sequence best reflects the approach?

options.text: Comply first, then report later if you are still concerned
Decline the action, offer an alternative, report if they insist or the matter is serious, and keep notes
Ignore the request and hope that it is not repeated, so that no one is put in a difficult position
Argue the point first, then comply if the colleague insists that it is necessary

questions.prompt: Why is it helpful to offer an alternative when you decline?

options.text: It avoids the need for any record
It turns the refusal into a legal matter
It makes the colleague more senior
It meets the real need and shows you are trying to help

questions.prompt: Which question helps you decide whether a request is acceptable?

options.text: Is the action quick to do?
Is the person friendly towards me?
Is the action permitted by policy?
Is the person senior to me?

questions.prompt: You already did what the senior person asked and now doubt it was right. What should you do?

options.text: Tell your manager or the security route that you were asked and did it
Delete the evidence of the request so that nobody else is affected by what happened
Ask the colleague to say nothing about it, so that neither of you is questioned
Hope it is not noticed and avoid the matter in future

questions.prompt: What protection exists if you raise a concern properly?

options.text: None, since the colleague is senior
Only if you are senior yourself
Only if the concern is proved correct
You should not be penalised for doing so

questions.prompt: Why keep dated notes of what you were asked?

options.text: They are required by law and have to be kept for ever on the department's central file
They provide a factual record if the matter is later questioned
They are shared with the colleague who made the request
They replace the need for any report to the security team, since they are already a record

questions.prompt: Which tone is best when declining a senior colleague?

options.text: Silent and vague
Angry and loud, so that others hear
Polite and brief, without accusation
Jokey and dismissive

questions.hint: Separate the issue from the person.

questions.prompt: How do senior people often receive a polite refusal?

options.text: With anger, as a challenge to their authority
Better than expected, since they too have a duty to listen
With discipline, as a refusal of an order given by a more senior member of staff
With silence, so that the matter is quietly dropped by both people

items.title: L9: Sharing data between teams and with outside bodies
items.source: UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018; ICO data sharing code of practice
items.body:
Requests to share personal data come from colleagues, other departments, researchers, the police and members of the public. Each tempts a quick answer, but judgement is needed.

The starting point is that personal data must be used lawfully, fairly and transparently, for a specified purpose, limited to what is necessary and kept secure. Sharing is a use of data, so it needs a lawful basis and a purpose compatible with why the data was collected. Sharing within a department may need a reason connected to the work; sharing with another body usually needs a documented arrangement, often a data sharing agreement, which sets out purpose, what is shared, security and how long.

Urgent requests are common. A genuine emergency, such as risk to life, may justify sharing quickly, and the law does not prevent it. But a request that is merely urgent, or from someone senior or official-sounding, is not enough on its own. Check who is asking, confirm by an independent route, ask what the purpose is, share the minimum, and record the decision.

Requests from the police or other authorities usually come through a formal process that your department's specialist team handles. Do not respond informally; pass the request to the team and tell the requester you have done so.

A person may also ask for their own data. This is a subject access request, and it goes to the data protection team, which has a legal time limit to respond. Do not decide it yourself.

When in doubt, pause and ask the data protection team. A short delay is better than an unlawful disclosure that cannot be undone.

questions.prompt: A colleague in another team asks for a full extract of customer records 'to save time'. What is the best response?

options.text: Send the full extract, since colleagues are trusted
Send a copy to a personal account first
Refuse to share anything with colleagues, ever
Ask what the purpose is, share only what is necessary, and check the basis with the data protection team if unsure

questions.prompt: Which feature usually accompanies sharing personal data with another body?

options.text: A documented arrangement setting out purpose, what is shared, security and duration
A record kept by the receiving body only, since the data is shared in good faith
A short note on a sticky label kept with the requester's papers
A verbal agreement made at a meeting between the two teams

questions.prompt: A phone call from someone claiming to be a senior official demands data urgently. What should you do?

options.text: Send it at once because of the urgency
Refuse to speak to anyone from outside the team
Ask them to send the request from a personal email
Check who is asking by an independent route, ask the purpose, share the minimum and record the decision

questions.prompt: Which situation can justify quick sharing of personal data?

options.text: A friendly request from a colleague
A senior person asking, since seniority gives authority to take the decision
A genuine emergency such as risk to life
A deadline set by a manager, since delay would affect the work

questions.prompt: The police ask you informally for a person's details by phone. What is the correct step?

options.text: Give only the address, which is less sensitive
Pass the request to the specialist team and tell the requester you have done so
Refuse and put the phone down
Give the details, since the request comes from the police

questions.prompt: A member of the public asks for a copy of the data held about them. How should this be handled?

options.text: As a subject access request, passed to the data protection team
By ignoring it, since the request was not made formally
By replying yourself with a copy of the file, as quickly as you can
By asking them to write to the press office, which deals with all outside requests

questions.prompt: Why is pausing to ask often better than sharing quickly?

options.text: Pausing is never allowed once a request is made
A short delay is better than an unlawful disclosure that cannot be undone
Sharing is always unlawful, so it must be avoided
Delays are always penalised, so quickness is the safe course

questions.prompt: Which principle limits the amount of data shared?

options.text: Data minimisation, meaning only what is necessary
Data aggregation, meaning all sources are combined
Data duplication, meaning copies are made for each user
Data maximisation, meaning everything that might be useful

questions.prompt: Which of these is a use of personal data that needs a lawful basis?

options.text: Reading it at your desk when your work requires it
Looking at it for your own curiosity
Sharing it with another body
Counting how many records there are

questions.prompt: What should you record when you decide to share data in an urgent case?

options.text: Only the name of the requester
Only the date on which the request was received
Nothing, since the urgency means there was no time to write it down
The decision, who asked, why, and what was shared

items.title: L9: Starting well: judgement in the first weeks
items.source: Civil Service Code; Civil Service Management Code; department induction guidance
items.body:
New staff face a mix of pressures: wanting to be helpful, not wanting to look foolish, and not yet knowing the unwritten rules. Good judgement in the first weeks is mostly about asking, declining politely and documenting.

Ask before assuming. If you are unsure whether you may share something, access something or take on something, ask your manager or the relevant team. New starters who ask are seen as careful. Decline politely when asked to do something outside the rules, even by someone more senior, and offer an approved alternative. Declare interests promptly: a second job, a family business, a friendship with someone you will be dealing with. Learn how to report: know who the security team, data protection team and nominated officers are on day one, so that you can act quickly when you need to.

Be careful with informal channels. Messaging apps and social media blur lines between private and official. Use approved tools for work. Do not discuss work in public places or on public transport. Be wary of unsolicited approaches online from people who show interest in your job.

Look after the paperwork. Complete mandatory learning and declarations on time, keep copies, note when you were told something, and record any arrangement made about your work.

If you make a mistake, report it. First-weeks mistakes are expected and forgiven when handled well, while concealed ones are treated seriously.

If you are unhappy about something, such as workload, unclear objectives or behaviour you have seen, raise it early with your manager or the routes the department offers. Probation is a time to learn, and your honesty and reliability are what will be judged most.

questions.prompt: On day three a colleague asks you to look up a friend's case 'just to check'. What should you do?

options.text: Do it quickly, since you are new and want to be helpful
Do it and tell no one, so that the colleague is not embarrassed
Decline, since you may access personal data only for a work purpose, and tell your manager if pressed
Do it, but only look at the first page of the record

questions.prompt: Why is it useful to know the security and data protection contacts on day one?

options.text: So that you can ask for early promotion on the strength of your contacts
So that you can act quickly if you need to report something
So that you can introduce yourself to senior staff
So that you can claim expenses correctly in your first month

questions.prompt: Which is the best way to handle a doubt about whether you may share something?

options.text: Ask your manager or the relevant team
Wait until you are more senior before deciding
